evidence.claim: The Prayut government continued to restrict freedom of expression and assembly in 2022, prosecuting human rights and democracy activists, community advocates, environmental defenders, and critics of the monarchy; HRW says at least 1,860 people had been prosecuted since mid-2020 and that the protest movement was disrupted by criminal prosecutions, crackdowns, and surveillance.
evidence.title: World Report 2023: Thailand
evidence.excerpt: The Prayut government continued to restrict freedom of expression and assembly in 2022, prosecuting human rights and democracy activists, community advocates, environmental defenders, and critics of the monarchy; HRW says at least 1,860 people had been prosecuted since mid-2020 and that the protest movement was disrupted by criminal prosecutions, crackdowns, and surveillance.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary annual country chapter by a major rights monitor summarizing 2022 with specific counts and attribution to the Prayut government.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers events of 2022 and the surrounding legal environment that shaped them.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Prime Minister Prayut Chan-o-cha and his government; this is office-level responsibility for the protest crackdown and associated legal regime.
contrary_evidence: This is broad pattern evidence rather than a single command order, and it includes continuity from 2020-2021.

evidence.claim: HRW says torture and enforced disappearance remained longstanding problems in Thailand, most reported cases were unresolved, and hardly anyone had been punished; it also notes abuses in the southern border provinces and during military custody persisted into the 2022 record.
evidence.title: World Report 2023: Thailand
evidence.excerpt: HRW says torture and enforced disappearance remained longstanding problems in Thailand, most reported cases were unresolved, and hardly anyone had been punished; it also notes abuses in the southern border provinces and during military custody persisted into the 2022 record.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct annual country chapter with specific findings on torture, disappearances, and accountability failure.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to 2022 because it summarizes the year-end safety and accountability environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attribution is to the Prayut government’s failure to secure accountability and protections within state custody and security operations.
contrary_evidence: The same report notes that the torture/disappearance bill was passed in August 2022, so the record is mixed rather than purely negative.

evidence.claim: In the southern border provinces, armed conflict subsided in early 2022 partly because the Thai military and BRN reduced violence during Ramadan, but attacks increased again from August despite ongoing dialogue; HRW says the government failed to prosecute security forces responsible for torture, unlawful killings, and other abuses of ethnic Malay Muslims, and often settled cases with compensation rather than accountability.
evidence.title: World Report 2023: Thailand
evidence.excerpt: In the southern border provinces, armed conflict subsided in early 2022 partly because the Thai military and BRN reduced violence during Ramadan, but attacks increased again from August despite ongoing dialogue; HRW says the government failed to prosecute security forces responsible for torture, unlawful killings, and other abuses of ethnic Malay Muslims, and often settled cases with compensation rather than accountability.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct country chapter with a specific 2022 conflict and accountability assessment in the south.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Prayut government because it maintained the relevant security and accountability regime; the violence itself is partly insurgent and therefore not wholly ruler-directed.
contrary_evidence: The report also notes dialogue and a Ramadan reduction in violence, so the record includes some de-escalatory steps.

evidence.claim: TLHR reported that, by the end of May 2022, at least 1,813 people in 1,074 cases had been prosecuted because of their expression and participation in demonstrations, including 280 minors, and that most charges involved Section 112 and emergency-decree cases.
evidence.title: Human Rights Situation Report May 2022: At least 1,813 individuals in 1,074 cases prosecuted
evidence.excerpt: TLHR reported that, by the end of May 2022, at least 1,813 people in 1,074 cases had been prosecuted because of their expression and participation in demonstrations, including 280 minors, and that most charges involved Section 112 and emergency-decree cases.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Local human-rights monitor with direct case-count documentation and date-specific reporting.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and highly specific to protest repression under Prayut.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Thai authorities under Prayut because the prosecutions were carried out by state institutions during his tenure.
contrary_evidence: The report shows some court acquittals and non-indictment decisions under the emergency decree, so enforcement was not uniform.

evidence.claim: HRW said two Thai pro-democracy activists were on hunger strike in 2022 because of prolonged pretrial detention on lese-majeste charges and urged the government to drop politically motivated cases; the article also notes that Prayut had ordered authorities in 2020 to restore lese-majeste prosecutions.
evidence.title: Thailand: Free Detained Critics of Monarchy
evidence.excerpt: HRW said two Thai pro-democracy activists were on hunger strike in 2022 because of prolonged pretrial detention on lese-majeste charges and urged the government to drop politically motivated cases; the article also notes that Prayut had ordered authorities in 2020 to restore lese-majeste prosecutions.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous rights monitoring with explicit attribution of the restored prosecution policy to Prayut.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and also useful as attributable continuity from prior policy into 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable at the policy level because the article ties the prosecutions to Prayut's 2020 order and the 2022 detentions flow from that regime.
contrary_evidence: This is protest/political-justice repression evidence rather than a physical-violence incident.

evidence.claim: The State Department said the Thai government restricted peaceful assembly, continued charging protesters under the COVID-19 emergency decree, sedition, and lese-majeste laws, and reported that 515 demonstrations occurred between January and August 2022.
evidence.title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Thailand
evidence.excerpt: The State Department said the Thai government restricted peaceful assembly, continued charging protesters under the COVID-19 emergency decree, sedition, and lese-majeste laws, and reported that 515 demonstrations occurred between January and August 2022.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary U.S. government human-rights report with explicit 2022 event counts and legal framing.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers the 2022 ruler-period and the protest environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Thai government under Prayut because it concerns national police and prosecutorial practice during his tenure.
contrary_evidence: The report also notes a constitutional right to assemble and some general access to bail, so the environment was repressive but not total closure.

evidence.claim: The State Department noted that the Thai government lifted the nationwide COVID-19-related emergency decree on October 1, 2022, ending the most obvious nationwide emergency tool even though critics said it had been used as a pretext to arrest anti-government protesters.
evidence.title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Thailand
evidence.excerpt: The State Department noted that the Thai government lifted the nationwide COVID-19-related emergency decree on October 1, 2022, ending the most obvious nationwide emergency tool even though critics said it had been used as a pretext to arrest anti-government protesters.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary U.S. government report summarizing a dated 2022 policy change and the surrounding criticism.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and materially relevant to emergency-power use.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Thai government under Prayut, though the report notes this was a nationwide policy shift rather than an individual order in the text.
contrary_evidence: The same report says the southern emergency decree and martial law remained in force, so this was only partial restraint.

evidence.claim: The report says the deep-south emergency decree and martial law gave security forces broad detention and search powers, limited access to counsel and family, and effectively provided immunity from criminal, civil, and disciplinary liability for officials acting under its provisions.
evidence.title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Thailand
evidence.excerpt: The report says the deep-south emergency decree and martial law gave security forces broad detention and search powers, limited access to counsel and family, and effectively provided immunity from criminal, civil, and disciplinary liability for officials acting under its provisions.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary U.S. government report describing the legal architecture of coercive control in the southern provinces.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to 2022 domestic safety and the inherited security regime.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Prayut government because it maintained the emergency and martial-law framework; however the regime predates him and is partly inherited.
contrary_evidence: The report does not prove misuse in every case and notes some steps to investigate and punish officials.

evidence.claim: HRW reported that Thai authorities detained 59 Rohingya who landed in Satun province, said the government treated Rohingya arriving at the border as illegal immigrants in indefinite immigration detention, and described a continuing pushback policy that could send boats onward rather than provide protection.
evidence.title: Thailand: Allow Newly Arrived Rohingya Access to Asylum
evidence.excerpt: HRW reported that Thai authorities detained 59 Rohingya who landed in Satun province, said the government treated Rohingya arriving at the border as illegal immigrants in indefinite immigration detention, and described a continuing pushback policy that could send boats onward rather than provide protection.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous rights reporting with specific numbers and explicit attribution to Thai state policy.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to vulnerable-group protection and detention policy.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Prayut government because it concerns border and immigration policy implemented by Thai authorities.
contrary_evidence: Thailand did provide some food, water, and shelter to specific arrivals, but the core policy remained detention and pushback.

evidence.claim: Amnesty said Thai authorities had intensified a years-long crackdown on child protesters through intimidation, surveillance, and criminalization, with police and officials monitoring dozens of children and pressuring family members and school authorities to discourage protest participation.
evidence.title: Thailand: Authorities must drop charges against child protesters
evidence.excerpt: Amnesty said Thai authorities had intensified a years-long crackdown on child protesters through intimidation, surveillance, and criminalization, with police and officials monitoring dozens of children and pressuring family members and school authorities to discourage protest participation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Amnesty report with direct allegations about monitoring, intimidation, and child-targeted criminalization.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and directly relevant to vulnerability and protest protection.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Thai police and government officials operating under Prayut's administration, not to a single local incident.
contrary_evidence: The source is advocacy-oriented and focuses on harmful conduct, so it does not capture any balancing remedial steps.

unresolved_gaps: No direct 2022 ruler-attributed existential-risk choice, escalation, or crisis-management episode is shown.
Command-and-control, custody, and safety-governance evidence tied specifically to Prayut remains thin.
PM-level attribution for 2022 international-security choices is still thin; most evidence is ministry or delegation posture.
The Myanmar and Ukraine material does not yet show concrete peace or accountability outcomes attributable to Prayut.
Direct chain-of-command evidence for the APEC crackdown and the deep-south emergency regime remains limited.
The torture/disappearance law is an important reform, but year-end enforcement evidence is still weak.
Direct evidence on the sponsors and mechanism of the election-system change is still thin.
4B.4 and 4B.7 remain under-evidenced relative to the stronger protest, media, and term-limit material.
Budget intent and macro recovery are better evidenced than actual implementation and take-up.
Evidence on appointments, anti-capture, and mistake-correction is still weak.
Direct service-delivery, take-up, and quality evidence is thin outside budget allocations and national surveys.
Ruler-specific causal attribution for rural, child, and mental-health outcomes remains weak.
No independent 2022 finding of personal lying, self-dealing, or concealed conflict of interest is shown.
The package relies too much on allegations, self-defense, and broader regime context.
The program basis is only partly explicit; some objectives are inferred from budgets and coalition moves rather than a single frozen program statement.
Outcome evidence is sectoral and mixed, and external reopening effects remain hard to separate from ruler skill.
